title: Zilch Commits £77m to Victoria HQ as European Expansion Accelerates
snippet: Zilch will take 33,160 sq ft at 40 Grosvenor Place on a 10-year lease, more than doubling capacity ahead of its planned Fjord The post Zilch Commits £77m to Victoria HQ as European Expansion Accelerates appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Zilch has signed a 10-year lease on a new London headquarters at 40 Grosvenor Place in Victoria, committing £77 million over the lease term and more than doubling its current office footprint. The buy-now-pay-later and payments platform will occupy floors four and five of the building, a 33,160 sq ft space the company says can accommodate more than 400 employees. Zilch expects to relocate from its current base at 111 Buckingham Palace Road in Spring 2027.

The investment manager for the building is PATRIZIA, represented by CBRE and Knight Frank, with XIX acting for Zilch.

A platform for European ambitions

Philip Belamant, CEO and co-founder at Zilch

The headquarters move sits alongside a cluster of strategic commitments that have changed the shape of the business this year. Zilch has announced the proposed acquisition of Fjord Bank, a deal that is expected to complete in the first half of 2027 and which the company says will form the foundation of its European expansion. It has also entered a multi-year strategic partnership with Visa and taken on a sponsorship arrangement as Arsenal FC’s official payments partner.

Cumulative customer spend on the Zilch platform has passed £8 billion across all UK regions, according to the company, and it counts six million customers on its books. Philip Belamant, co-founder and chief executive, said the new headquarters reflects “the scale of our ambition and the momentum behind our growth” and described the site as a base for attracting talent both domestically and internationally.

City Minister Lucy Rigby KC MP welcomed the announcement, describing the UK as “a fintech powerhouse” and voicing support for the sector’s continued growth.

Market and regulatory context

The Fjord Bank acquisition, once completed, would give Zilch a European banking licence and materially alter its regulatory footprint. For a BNPL provider that has operated largely under consumer-credit exemptions, holding a licensed deposit-taking entity in Europe carries both an opportunity and a compliance cost: greater product range and cross-border reach, but also capital requirements, prudential reporting obligations and exposure to the evolving Consumer Credit Directive framework across EU member states.

The broader BNPL sector has been navigating tightening oversight on both sides of the Channel. In the UK, the Treasury’s long-running consultation on bringing BNPL within the FCA regulatory perimeter has yet to conclude in final rules, though industry participants have been preparing for credit-authorisation requirements for several years. A banking licence acquired through Fjord Bank could allow Zilch to pre-empt some of that regulatory uncertainty by operating within an already-licenced structure.

Competitively, the move mirrors a pattern seen among better-capitalised BNPL players globally: consolidation upward into banking infrastructure rather than remaining as a merchant-facing credit layer. Klarna‘s pursuit of a public listing and Affirm’s continued push into debit and banking products reflect the same structural logic. Zilch’s Visa partnership adds an acceptance-network dimension that standalone BNPL products lack, potentially supporting the “intelligent payments platform” positioning the company has adopted as a framing that goes beyond instalment credit.

The Victoria headquarters lease is a long-duration fixed commitment, which signals confidence in the London talent market and the company’s trajectory. The proof of that conviction will come when the Fjord Bank deal closes and Zilch moves to convert the European banking licence into live product revenue.

title: Dubai Fintech Summit day two: 2,000 firms, a Japanese bridge and AI moves into production
snippet: The Dubai Fintech Summit closed its second day at Madinat Jumeirah on Tuesday with DIFC marking a milestone it set itself less than ten years ago. The centre is now home to more than 2,000 AI, fintech and innovation firms The post Dubai Fintech Summit day two: 2,000 firms, a Japanese bridge and AI moves into production appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
DIFC passed 2,000 AI, fintech and innovation firms and opened its doors to Japanese startups, the case for careful tokenisation, and the region’s banks showed how far AI has moved from pilot to production. Under it all ran a question about who, or what, the next customer will be.

The Dubai Fintech Summit closed its second day at Madinat Jumeirah on Tuesday with DIFC marking a milestone it set itself less than ten years ago. The centre is now home to more than 2,000 AI, fintech and innovation firms, His Excellency Arif Amiri, chief executive of DIFC Authority, told the opening plenary, up from the 11 startups that joined its first accelerator in 2017.

From 11 startups to 2,000 firms

Amiri said the number that matters is not how many firms arrive but how many grow from Dubai into global leaders. He used the stage to set out two new pieces. A partnership will give up to 6,000 Japanese startups direct access to the DIFC ecosystem, part of a wider push into emerging markets and new corridors with the Global South. DIFC will also launch a Dubai Fintech Stack, a set of tools to help founders with onboarding, payments, risk, security and AI. Neither the Japanese partner nor a launch date was named.

The day’s big numbers came from Digital Economy 2.0, a report DIFC published with Asia House. Michael Lawrence, Asia House’s chief executive, told the summit that the digital economy is moving on from digitising processes to systems that act for themselves. The report puts global technology spending at USD 5.6trn this year and expects AI to add USD 22.3trn to the world economy by 2030, while the fintech market grows from around USD 400bn today to USD 1.5trn. Lawrence set Dubai beside Singapore and Switzerland’s Zug and Zurich as the hubs to watch, and urged businesses to move post-quantum cryptography up their agenda, with cybercrime already costing the world about USD 10trn a year. The next report in the series, on the strategic business hubs of tomorrow, is due on 25 November.

Tokenisation as evolution, not revolution

Noel Quinn, chair of Julius Baer and former group chief executive of HSBC, gave the summit’s signature session, a nod to Julius Baer having been the first financial firm to set up in DIFC, in 2004. He called tokenisation a natural evolution rather than a revolution, and asked the room to separate the blockchain from the products built on it. The bigger prize, he argued, is opening assets such as bonds, gold and trade finance to investors who could not reach them before, with a full audit trail behind every slice.

He was just as clear about the limits. Enthusiasm for the technology is no substitute for due diligence, and a crypto hack earlier this week was not a failure of the chain itself. “It wasn’t the blockchain that got hacked. It was the entry point to the blockchain that got hacked in a very old-fashioned way,” he said.

On AI, Quinn recalled how HSBC used it to cut complex multi-currency pricing from hours to minutes while leaving the final call with the trader, and said AI will become part of every bank’s technology stack, not least to screen payments for money laundering and sanctions.

He was followed by Dr Fatih Karahan, Governor of the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye, who set out how far Turkey has come: reserves rebuilt, USD 140bn of FX-protected deposit liabilities run down to zero, and inflation down from a peak of 75 per cent to just under 30 per cent. He made the case for payment sovereignty, pointing to the central bank’s own settlement and instant payment systems, and said Turkey is joining SEPA and SWIFT’s new instant payments scheme.

Banks move AI into production

Away from the plenary, the region’s banks talked less about whether to use AI and more about how much of the bank it can now run. Miguel Rio-Tinto, who leads digital and technology at Emirates NBD, told The Fintech Times the bank has more than 150 AI initiatives under way, 65 of them already in production. Customers who call the bank are answered by an AI agent, and an agent inside the ENBD X app will soon replace its menus. The bank builds and orchestrates its customer journeys itself, with some 2,500 software engineers, but partners for frontier models and for the computing power to run them.

Cyber security is where he sees the sharpest change. As frontier models get better at finding software flaws, the number of critical vulnerabilities the bank has to assess has risen from about 1,000 a month at the start of 2025 to around 15,000 in October, he said. Emirates NBD is answering with the same tools, using a frontier model from its recently announced OpenAI partnership to probe its own systems. For Rio-Tinto, the choice echoes the bank’s earlier digital drive. “Our CEO was constantly hammering us, digitise or die. The same thing is happening now. It’s AI or die,” he said. [VIDEO: Miguel Rio-Tinto, Emirates NBD]

Commercial Bank of Dubai, the summit’s strategic banking partner, used the week to sign a run of agreements: with Microsoft on AI use cases, Silent Eight on AI name screening, Comarch on its digital wealth platform, Zamp on intelligent automation, and Harvey, Sirion and Flank on legal technology. Thomas Cherian, the bank’s chief technology and services officer, said its Merlin platform, which drafts credit proposals in minutes, is now used by 85 per cent of relationship managers in wholesale banking. He believes 55 to 60 per cent of operations work could be handed to AI agents, with a person still approving the outcome, and the bank wants to own the agents it builds and the IP behind them. His warning was about where to start. “If you try to automate what you have today, I don’t think you will get anything out of it,” he said. [VIDEO: Thomas Cherian, Commercial Bank of Dubai]

Rails for agents, and for corridors

For Zand Bank, the next customer may not be human at all. Chief executive Michael Chan said the bank set up its blockchain and AI teams 30 months ago to prepare for agentic commerce, in which AI agents pay each other on chain using stablecoins, custody and tokenised assets. On-chain volumes are climbing fast, with one recent single transaction worth USD 100m, and he expects agentic commerce to arrive within 12 months. He sees demand well beyond business payments, pointing to people in Africa hit by currency devaluation who need faster access to dollars. The obstacle, in his view, is not technical. “Technology is never the problem. I think it’s the synchronisation, alignment between the different jurisdictions that is the biggest problem we have to solve,” he said. [VIDEO: Michael Chan, Zand Bank]

MultiBank Group founder and chairman Naser Taher brought the corridor theme from the east. After two decades in China, he moved the group’s interbank trading platform project from Hong Kong to the UAE, where it now has government backing and is aimed at BRICS and emerging markets, with settlement offered in stablecoins including USDU, a UAE-based dollar stablecoin. He expects traditional finance, digital assets and AI to fold into a single super app within a year or two. “They have to merge. 100 per cent, they have to merge,” he said. [VIDEO: Naser Taher, MultiBank Group]

Beyond the summit

Tuesday also widened the week beyond fintech. At the Future Sustainability Forum, DIFC said partners in its 1 Million Learners programme have reached more than 130,000 people this year, and that it is building a Total Impact Framework with a certified B Corp consultancy to measure outcomes. Space for Earth Labs, its geospatial accelerator with the Mohammed Bin Rashid Space Centre and RELM Insurance, drew 73 applications from 24 countries. IPEM Future made its Dubai debut, InsureTek opened its two-day run.

Dubai Future Finance Week continues on Wednesday with the Future Islamic Finance Forum at Madinat Jumeirah.

title: The Endgame of Cross-Border Payments Is an Operating System
snippet: PhotonPay argues that global B2B payments need a Financial OS combining fiat and stablecoin rails, FX and APIs to simplify cross-border money movement and make global commerce more accessible. The post The Endgame of Cross-Border Payments Is an Operating System appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Today, a global business can use sophisticated SaaS to manage customers, AI to improve operations, and ERP systems to track orders and inventory in real time.

Lewison Chen, founder & CEO at PhotonPay

But the moment money needs to move across markets, the experience can feel as if the business has stepped back into another era.

Companies still need to open accounts across jurisdictions, connect with different banks and payment providers, understand local clearing systems, navigate compliance requirements, manage FX and cut-off times, and reconcile transactions across disconnected systems.

Business operations have moved to the cloud. Money movement, in many ways, is still running on bare metal.

That is why I increasingly believe the missing layer in B2B cross-border payments is not another bank account, another wallet, or even another payment method.

What is missing is a financial operating system.

From Connecting More Networks to Abstracting Complexity

The breakthrough of an operating system was never about teaching everyone how processors, memory, and motherboards work.

It was the opposite.

Windows and macOS created value by abstracting the complexity of the underlying hardware, allowing people to use applications and get work done without understanding every component underneath.

Global money movement is approaching the same transition.

For years, the payments industry has focused on connectivity: connecting more banks, more markets, more currencies, and more payment methods. Those connections still matter. But as businesses become truly global, adding more connections is no longer enough.

The next generation of financial infrastructure must answer a different question: How do we make all that complexity manageable without making businesses navigate it themselves?

A true Financial OS needs to connect to bank accounts, local clearing systems, card networks, foreign exchange infrastructure, and emerging stablecoin rails, while abstracting their different rules, formats, settlement windows, and liquidity requirements into one unified infrastructure layer.

The experience above that layer should become radically simpler.

One account architecture.

One view of liquidity.

One set of APIs.

A business should not need to know which correspondent bank handled a transaction, which domestic clearing network was used, or which settlement rail was selected behind the scenes.

It should only need to express intent:

How much money needs to move, from where, to where, and by when?

The infrastructure should take care of the rest.

Fiat and Stablecoins Should Not Be a Binary Choice

When global payment infrastructure is discussed today, the conversation is often framed as a binary choice:

Fiat represents the legacy system. Stablecoins represent the future.

I do not believe that is how real commerce evolves.

Businesses do not abandon an entire financial system overnight because a new technology becomes available. They still need to pay employees and suppliers, collect from customers, settle invoices, pay taxes, and ultimately operate within local economies.

For B2B payments, fiat is not a legacy system waiting to disappear. It remains one of the fundamental anchors of global commerce.

The global account, local collection and payout capabilities, FX infrastructure, card capabilities, and systems such as Matrix that PhotonPay has built over the years form an important fiat foundation for this operating system. They address the most fundamental questions businesses face when entering a market: how to hold, collect, convert, pay, and manage money in compliance with local requirements.

At the same time, traditional banking and clearing infrastructure operates within established schedules and processes. Business-day windows, payment cut-off times, and the need to manage liquidity across markets can all affect how quickly money becomes available for use.

This is where stablecoins become strategically important.

Their role is not to move businesses into a purely crypto-native world. They can provide an additional 24/7 rail for moving value across borders, complementing the banking and payment infrastructure businesses already rely on.

I believe these two systems will increasingly operate as complementary components of the same financial operating system, rather than competing alternatives that force businesses to choose one over the other.

 The Real Value Is Not Adding Another Stablecoin Rail

If a customer still has to decide when to use a bank network, when to acquire stablecoins, and when to convert back into fiat, we have not actually reduced complexity.

We have simply added another layer of it.

The value of an operating system lies in orchestration.

Imagine a company needs to move liquidity from Asia to Latin America. For the business, this should be a straightforward commercial instruction. Behind the scenes, however, the infrastructure may need to evaluate available liquidity, foreign exchange rates, settlement windows, costs, fund availability, and compliance requirements across multiple markets before determining an appropriate route.

In some cases, the most suitable path may run entirely through traditional banking rails. In others, stablecoins may serve as an intermediate value-transfer layer:

Local fiat → digital value transfer → destination fiat.

The business can continue operating in the fiat environment it already understands, while stablecoins become part of the underlying infrastructure rather than an additional process the customer must manage.

That is what multi-rail financial infrastructure should ultimately mean. The objective is not simply to give businesses more routes, but to coordinate those routes around their operating needs.

The customer should not have to choose the rail. The system should.

APIs Allow Money to Operate More Like Software

Once the underlying networks are abstracted, the change is not simply about faster payments.

It changes how a company can organize money itself.

In traditional financial operations, many treasury workflows remain highly manual. Teams log into different banking portals, download statements, check balances, initiate transfers, wait for approvals, and reconcile data back into internal systems.

APIs do more than improve one of these steps. They allow financial workflows to become programmable.

When payment infrastructure is embedded directly into a company’s ERP, treasury system, marketplace, or SaaS platform, money can begin responding automatically to business events.

An order is completed. Funds are allocated according to predefined rules.

A supplier reaches a payment milestone. A payment can be triggered through an authorized workflow.

Liquidity falls below a threshold in one market. The system can initiate a rebalancing process.

A transaction settles. Reconciliation data flows back into the company’s systems.

At that point, payments are no longer merely a back-office process sitting outside the business. They become part of the software through which the business operates.

This is an important step toward a Financial OS: financial capabilities can be called when the business needs them, under rules defined by the business, rather than requiring people to coordinate every operational step manually.

But Every Financial OS Must Answer a More Important Question: What Is It For?

Technology can easily make an industry obsessed with capability.

Faster. More networks. More assets. More sophisticated routing.

But infrastructure does not exist to demonstrate infrastructure. It must ultimately serve real commerce.

Today, PhotonPay serves more than 200,000 businesses across more than 200 countries and territories. They span cross-border commerce, SaaS, digital services, entertainment, and an increasing number of traditional industries expanding internationally.

The problems they face are often remarkably practical.

A supplier needs to receive funds today.

Employees across dozens of markets need to be paid on time.

An overseas advertising account suddenly requires additional liquidity.

Or a fast-growing company enters its fifth or tenth market and realizes that its existing financial architecture can no longer support the pace of expansion.

These everyday realities are why financial infrastructure matters.

Our focus is not capital movement in isolation. It is helping businesses build products, provide services, employ people, purchase goods, and serve customers around the world.

Real commerce is the anchor of this Financial OS.

The Next Phase of Globalization Will Be Plug-and-Play

Historically, becoming a multinational company meant building a multinational organization.

Banking relationships, finance teams, payment providers, local entities, and treasury infrastructure often had to be rebuilt market by market. That made globalization disproportionately accessible to companies with the greatest resources.

But software has repeatedly demonstrated a different pattern:

Once a complex capability becomes infrastructure, something that was once available only to the largest organizations can become a service accessible to almost any company.

Cloud computing did this.

Communications did this.

AI is doing it now.

Global financial infrastructure can follow the same trajectory.

In the future, entering a new market should require less rebuilding of a company’s financial stack. It could increasingly mean connecting to a new API, enabling another module, or activating another asset or settlement rail within an existing system.

Global financial infrastructure can become increasingly plug-and-play.

That is why we are building PhotonPay as the next-generation Financial OS for global commerce.

Our $40 million Series C, led by Blockchain Capital with participation from SBI Group and continued support from existing investors, will help accelerate this work. Our ambition is not to build another payment method or simply expand a global network of accounts. It is to create a financial infrastructure layer that is stable, open, and increasingly intelligent, allowing businesses to move and deploy value globally without having to navigate every layer of complexity underneath.

Global commerce is entering a new phase of competition.

Speed is no longer simply about how quickly a payment arrives. What matters is how quickly a company can enter a market, mobilize liquidity, respond to change, and continue growing without allowing operational complexity to grow at the same pace.the fin

The best infrastructure ultimately becomes almost invisible.

Today, few people think about how a CPU allocates resources every time they open an application. In the future, businesses should not have to reconsider the underlying path of money every time value moves across borders.

They should focus on running their business.

The OS should handle the rest.

About PhotonPay

Founded in Hong Kong in 2015, PhotonPay is a global fintech company building a next-generation, stablecoin-centric Financial Operating System (Financial OS). Its API-first architecture brings together multi-asset wallets supporting stablecoins and fiat currencies, global money movement, foreign exchange, global card issuing, embedded finance, and local clearing infrastructure, connecting digital and traditional financial rails within an integrated financial system.

In October 2026, PhotonPay announced a $40 million Series C funding round led by Blockchain Capital, with participation from new investor SBI Group and follow-on investments from existing investors IDG Capital, GL Ventures, and Lightspeed Faction.

PhotonPay operates 16 offices worldwide, employs nearly 600 people, and holds 34 payment and financial licenses and regulatory authorizations across the Americas, Europe and Asia. The company serves businesses across more than 200 countries and territories.

For more information, visit www.photonpay.com

FCA to explore quantum computing to tackle financial crime

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing.

  

            						

The FCA will bring together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore how quantum computing could help tackle financial crime.

The Quantum Experimentation Group, the first of its kind for a regulator, will initially explore how quantum machine learning could help detect money laundering and fraud. It will launch in the first quarter of 2027.

Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset – artificially generated data – to help overcome a key barrier to testing: access to suitable data.

The group will help firms explore practical uses of quantum computing in financial services and share findings to guide future testing. It will also help the FCA understand the technology’s opportunities and limitations, barriers to experimentation and what these could mean for regulation.

Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'We want to help firms explore where quantum could make a meaningful difference, and early experimentation is essential to understanding its potential in financial services. By bringing together firms, technology providers and researchers we can build readiness and identify practical applications for common industry challenges, starting with financial crime.'

The initiative builds on the FCA’s research into the long-term potential of quantum computing in financial services.

Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in joining the group by 31 December 2026.

Notes to editors

Read more about the Quantum Experimentation Group and how to register an interest in joining the group.

The FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will be the world’s first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group.

The group will support organisations at different stages of their quantum journey, from those beginning to explore potential use cases to those already undertaking advanced experimentation.

As part of the initiative, the FCA will define problem statements and work alongside participants to build understanding of the opportunities, limitations and practical considerations associated with quantum technologies.

The initiative will complement wider activity across the UK’s quantum ecosystem by creating additional opportunities for collaborative experimentation and learning.

title: Dubai Future Finance Week day three: 600 wealth firms, a Mizuho bridge and Islamic finance’s connection problem
snippet: Dubai Future Finance Week moved its focus from fintech to wealth, fixed income, insurance and Islamic finance. DIFC began the day with another milestone. The centre is now home to more than 600 wealth and asset management firm The post Dubai Future Finance Week day three: 600 wealth firms, a Mizuho bridge and Islamic finance’s connection problem appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
DIFC passed 600 wealth and asset management firms and named Mizuho as its partner for Japanese startups. At the Future Islamic Finance Forum, the industry’s own leaders gave a frank verdict: there is no shortage of capital or goodwill, but markets, institutions and fintechs are still too poorly connected.

On Wednesday, Dubai Future Finance Week moved its focus from fintech to wealth, fixed income, insurance and Islamic finance. DIFC began the day with another milestone. The centre is now home to more than 600 wealth and asset management firms, well ahead of any other centre in the region by its own count, as family offices and institutional investors set up regional headquarters in Dubai. The DealCatalyst Fixed Income Alternatives programme brought European and US asset managers and structured credit investors together with regional banks and sovereign funds to discuss private credit, structured finance and new funding models.

A name for the Japanese bridge

The Japanese partnership that Arif Amiri, chief executive of DIFC Authority, trailed on stage on Tuesday now has a name. DIFC has signed a strategic partnership with Mizuho Financial Group that will give up to 6,000 of the bank’s startup clients access to the DIFC Innovation Hub and Ignyte, its digital innovation platform, with market entry and soft landing support across the Middle East, Africa and South Asia. Amiri signed for DIFC and Suneel Bakhshi, deputy group CEO, signed for Mizuho, with DIFC Governor Essa Kazim as witness.

The deal builds on a 20-year relationship. DIFC hosts the UAE’s only cluster of Japanese financial firms, 19 companies employing 560 people, including Mizuho, SMBC, MUFG, Nomura and the Japan Bank for International Cooperation. Mizuho says it has provided around JPY 1trn in financing to Japanese startups over the past three years and has more than 400 specialists supporting them. The partnership will focus on AI upskilling, Fintech, digital transformation and cross-border links.

Islamic finance at 50

More than 1,000 people from over 50 countries came to the Future Islamic Finance Forum at Madinat Jumeirah, and DIFC used it to launch three initiatives. DIFC Academy is opening learning pathways through its Centre for Global Islamic Finance, aiming for more than 3,000 learners by 2031. The Islamic Finance Innovation Challenge by Ignyte will pair Islamic banks with technology ventures to pilot production-ready tools for financing, sukuk structuring, compliance and takaful. And the DIFC Innovation Hub will set up an Islamic Finance Innovation Centre with CRDB Bank, Emirates Islamic, Principle Investor Group and Standard Chartered Saadiq. The centre will bring banks, regulators, Shariah scholars, standards bodies and technology firms together to work on shared problems, with a focus on the Global South. DIFC puts the Islamic finance industry at USD 9.31trn by 2030 and Islamic fintech at close to USD 180bn this year.

The leadership panel opened with a reminder of how far the industry has come. Mustafa Adil, head of Islamic finance at LSEG, noted that modern Islamic finance is about 50 years old and began in Dubai. It now holds more than USD 6trn in assets across over 2,200 institutions in more than 80 countries, and 56 countries have Islamic finance rules of some kind. It is also concentrated in a few markets that still work largely in silos.

Khurram Hilal, group chief executive of Standard Chartered Saadiq, argued that the next phase depends on connection: between banking, asset management and philanthropy within the industry, and between regions outside it. He said the industry has looked west for too long and should become a bridge across the Global South, especially between East Asia and the Gulf. “There’s a lot more conversations that need to take place between the East and West of Asia,” he said. He described a Middle East roadshow in Beijing this year where the central bank, the sovereign wealth fund and corporates were all keen to explore Islamic finance, and said the industry needs to reach out more.

Sukuk: big, but bunched up

Hilal was blunt about sukuk. The market passed USD 1trn, he said, but around 80 per cent of it sits in the GCC and Malaysia. Sovereigns and financial institutions account for roughly 95 per cent of issuers, and less than 6 per cent of the capital raised reaches Africa or South Asia, where infrastructure needs are greatest. Because supply is short, holders keep their paper and the secondary market stays thin. He pointed to growing Shariah-compliant repo volumes and an IIFM project to standardise repo documents as ways to free up trapped liquidity. He also said this year’s regional conflict showed the need for proper hedging tools for institutions concentrated in one market.

Charles Haresnape, chief executive of Gatehouse Bank, spoke about the UK and Europe, where 45 million Muslims in Europe and 6 million in the UK remain underserved. Gatehouse campaigned successfully for equal tax treatment for some Islamic products, but the UK did not renew its sovereign sukuk this year, so the bank has to buy overseas paper for its liquidity buffers. “There isn’t one, which is crazy,” he said. He also said about half of Gatehouse’s customers are not Muslim, younger customers see Islamic and sustainable finance as much the same thing, and the portfolios it sells are bought mainly by conventional investors.

Professor Talal Yassine, managing director of Australia’s Salaam, which manages a Shariah-compliant pension fund of around AUD 750m, described the opposite lesson on marketing. Pitching to ethical and Islamic investors at once, he said, ended up selling to nobody. Speaking in Islamic terms has gone down better with regulators and customers. He also said the industry’s money is out of step with the wider halal economy. Nurym Ayazbayev, executive director for Islamic finance at the Eurasian Development Bank, said the UAE provided USD 15.5bn of the USD 22.8bn in direct investment into Central Asia by mid 2025. The region now has four full Islamic banks and more than ten Islamic windows, and the bank has opened an office in Abu Dhabi to be closer to Gulf capital.

Fintech’s graduation problem

A second panel looked at why Islamic fintech struggles to scale. Mohammad Kamran Wajid, deputy chief executive of Emirates Islamic, said banks, regulators, investors and fintechs pursue different goals in separate silos. Even an Islamic window and an Islamic bank in the same group can have separate Shariah boards, he said. His bank’s e-KYC pilot with a fintech stalled over compliance and fraud, and he suggested banks share platforms instead of each reinventing the wheel.

Iqbal Khan, chief executive of Fajr Capital, said capital is not the constraint but scale is. Very few fintechs get past about USD 20m in revenue. Under bank capital rules, venture stakes carry risk weights that keep Islamic banks out, and exit routes are limited. He called for a mezzanine fund to carry companies from startup to maturity, and for banks to separate payments from lending. For his firm, Shariah has to be central to a business. “Sharia is not seen as a bolt-on. Sharia is authentic,” he said.

For the regulator, Eisa Al Amri, associate director for macro-prudential supervision at the DFSA, said rules become a burden when they are unclear, and uncertainty is expensive. “We don’t regulate the technology per se, but what we do is we look at the activity and the risks associated with that activity,” he said. He pointed to the DFSA’s Innovation Testing Licence for startups and to a bank that had never held a digital custody permission anywhere and got one in DIFC after early engagement. On Shariah, he said the DFSA checks that a firm has the right governance in place, while rulings remain a matter for the firm’s own board.

Dr Mughees Shaukat, managing director of Panacea Consulting, put it more sharply. He argued that forcing agile fintechs into bureaucratic banks is the wrong model, and that asset managers, capital markets and venture investors should do more of the lifting. Shariah standards can take two to three years to produce, far too slow for technology, so he proposed a dedicated body to set fast-track standards for digital finance and fintech. He said Oman is building its own international financial centre, modelled on Astana’s AIFC.

Dubai Future Finance Week continues on Thursday with the Future Tokenisation Forum at Jumeirah Mina Al Salam, where regulators including the DFSA and VARA take the stage, alongside the Dubai Family Wealth Summit and the Investment Leaders Exchange.

title: Animoca and Franklin Templeton Bring Tokenised RWAs to NUVA
snippet: Franklin Templeton will bring institutional-grade tokenised real-world assets to NUVA, the Animoca Brands-backed vault marketplace, widening its asset base. The post Animoca and Franklin Templeton Bring Tokenised RWAs to NUVA appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Animoca Brands and Franklin Templeton have struck a strategic collaboration to bring tokenised real-world assets to NUVA, the Animoca Brands-backed vault marketplace, with the aim of widening institutional access to tokenised investment products.

Yat Siu, co-founder and executive chairman at Animoca Brands

The tie-up extends NUVA beyond the assets it already offers on the Provenance blockchain, opening it to institutional-grade assets from a broader base of issuers. NUVA was co-incubated by Animoca Brands and Nuva Labs and launched in May 2026 with vaults giving access to assets on Provenance, which held more than USD 30 billion in total value locked as of 24 September 2026.

The market capitalisation of tokenised assets has kept climbing since mid-September, despite the CLARITY Act failing to advance in the US Senate, and large financial institutions are increasingly choosing to partner with established digital asset firms rather than build alone.

Yat Siu, co-founder and executive chairman of Animoca Brands, said: “The convergence of traditional finance and digital assets has gone from the theoretical to being a real infrastructure play. Franklin Templeton is a pioneer in tokenizing traditional financial assets, and this partnership allows us to integrate institutional-grade RWAs directly into NUVA’s vault architecture.”

Beyond putting assets on chain

Franklin Templeton, which manages USD 1.83 trillion in assets as of 31 August 2026, sees the next stage of tokenisation as being about how assets are used once they are on chain.

“Tokenization is moving beyond simply putting traditional assets on blockchain rails. The next phase is about expanding how those assets can be accessed, utilized and integrated into increasingly digital investment ecosystems,” said Sandy Kaul, head of digital assets and innovation at Franklin Templeton.

The two firms have also published a four-part, co-authored research series on what tokenisation means for institutional investors, how the market reached its current point and how it is changing the way institutions assess assets and build portfolios.

They plan to look at further areas of collaboration, including the co-design and tokenisation of real-world cultural assets, with more details expected later this year. Animoca Brands, whose portfolio spans more than 600 companies and digital assets including OpenSea, Ledger and Kraken, has positioned itself as an early mover in the space.

fullText:
Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.

The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.

Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.

That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. We don’t know for certain when a viable quantum computer will emerge, but the coming years will likely see the technology advance at a rapid pace.

Preparing for this new world requires firms to understand where and how they use cryptography and to be able to migrate all hardware and software to PQC, while managing operational risks.

Realistically, for most firms, this will require significant time, investment and effort.

What firms need to do now

So, what kind of timescale are we talking about? The National Centre for Cyber Security (NCSC) recommends 3 key milestones:

By 2028, firms complete a PQC migration plan.

By 2031, firms carry out high-priority migration activities.

By 2035, firms have migrated all systems, services and products to PQC.

Firms should not wait for these milestones before acting and where it is safe to do so, they should seek to be ready sooner. In line with NCSC guidance, we expect firms to act now to: 

Have a thorough and accurate understanding of the cryptography in place across systems and information.

Set clear, achievable, safe and risk-based migration objectives..

Implement migration plans and monitor, test and validate the changes, adjusting them where necessary.

Senior managers should ensure that their firms allocate enough time, investment and resources to manage PQC migration safely and meet the relevant deadlines. Failed change projects accounted for around a fifth of all incidents reported to us in 2025.

How we are supporting firms

We are trialling a new supervisory self-assessment tool with an initial sample of firms and intend to extend it to other firms in due course. This will help firms assess the maturity of their plans and help us understand the industry’s preparedness for PQC migration.

This trial will also help us identify common challenges and examples of good practice, which we intend to share with the sector.

We shared relevant insights from firms in April 2026 and will continue to engage with the industry through our Cyber Coordination Groups (CCGs), the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), and trade bodies and associations.

We will also consult on cyber resilience guidance for firms, including our expectations for how firms should address PQC risks through their cryptographic controls.

You can find more information:

NCSC, Timelines for migration to post-quantum cryptography 

G7 Cyber Expert Group, Statement on advancing a coordinated roadmap for the transition to post-quantum cryptography in the financial sector 

CMORG, Guidance for post-quantum cryptography

title: Binance’s $6.3bn hack: one laptop, and a warning for every bank
snippet: Binance's record $6.3bn hack began with one engineer's laptop. Security, custody and markets experts say every bank should take the lesson personally. The post Binance’s $6.3bn hack: one laptop, and a warning for every bank appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The largest crypto theft on record did not break a blockchain. It started, Binance believes, on one engineer’s laptop, and the attackers then used the exchange’s own approval process to move about $6.3 billion in roughly 20 minutes.

Security, fraud, custody and markets specialists who sent reaction to The Fintech Times agree on the lesson, and most of them say it is not only crypto’s to learn.

What happened

Attackers drained Binance hot wallets on ten blockchains on the afternoon of 29 October, US Eastern time. Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs puts the total at about $6.36 billion and links the attack to North Korea, as does Chainalysis. That is more than four times the previous record, the roughly $1.5 billion taken from Bybit in February 2025.

Binance’s initial investigation pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop that gave the attacker access to a service container, from which unauthorised withdrawal transactions were submitted. The exchange said it found no evidence that a wallet private key had leaked. Stablecoin issuers moved quickly: Tether and Circle froze around $3 billion of the stolen funds.

Binance suspended deposits and withdrawals for about 45 hours, pledged to cover all losses from its Secure Asset Fund for Users and its own balance sheet, and by 1 November said it had replenished about 95 per cent of the affected assets. When withdrawals reopened on 1 November, customers took out $4.65 billion against $1.01 billion of deposits in the first nine and a half hours, a net outflow of $3.64 billion, according to figures reported by CoinDesk. Binance published a fresh proof of reserves snapshot on 2 November and has scheduled another for 4 November. Bitcoin fell below $80,000 as the news spread and was trading around $77,000 on 2 November.

It started with a laptop

For Nauman Abuzar, VP of risk and compliance at fraud prevention firm SEON, the point of entry is the story. “Once the attacker gained that access, the transactions appeared valid to the systems processing them, and funds moved across multiple blockchains in minutes. That leaves very little time to intervene,” he said. “Controls that only kick in once a transaction starts may already be too late. Teams need to identify compromised access early, whether that’s a new device, an unusual login pattern or an employee account suddenly behaving differently, and connect those signals to what is happening with the funds.”

Javvad Malik, lead CISO advisor at KnowBe4, said the most catastrophic breaches “rarely exploit exotic zero-days in core protocols, but instead hinge on privileged access failures.” His prescription: “Leaders need to build walls between everyday work laptops and core financial systems, require multiple independent people to sign off before large amounts of money can leave the building, and set automatic spending caps that immediately freeze suspicious, high-volume transactions before the damage is done.”

Chris Dimitriadis, chief global strategy officer at ISACA, the professional body for digital trust, put it more bluntly, calling the attack “a stark reminder that you can spend a fortune protecting your most critical systems, but if just one device is compromised, then your security is only as strong as the weakest machine on the network.” Organisations holding high-value assets, he said, “must assume a breach will happen and plan for it ahead of time.”

Georgy Kucherin, senior security researcher at Kaspersky‘s Global Research and Analysis Team, said technical staff at exchanges remain a favoured route in, and that “even experienced engineers and developers can become victims of cyberattacks and, in some cases, inadvertently download malware.” He cautioned that North Korea’s Lazarus group is among the suspects but that its involvement “remains under examination and final conclusions can only be drawn once the investigation is complete.”

Banks learned this in 2016

Stefan Deiss, CEO of The Hashgraph Group, a Swiss identity infrastructure company, called it an identity problem rather than a crypto one: “once a system believes you are someone it trusts, it lets you act.” He drew the parallel with the attempt by North Korean hackers to move nearly $1 billion out of Bangladesh’s central bank in 2016, after which banks tightened controls “so that no single login can move large sums without independent checks. Crypto has grown so quickly that its security has focused on protecting the blockchain itself, while controls around the people and systems inside the business have been slower to catch up.”

Several respondents said traditional finance should not treat this as someone else’s problem. Deep Patel, partner and UK payments lead at consultancy Capco, noted that “many mainstream financial services organisations are in the midst of delivering exchange and wallet capability, and will no doubt now be taking a moment to pause and review cybersecurity designs and controls.”

Analysts at GlobalData said attackers “are increasingly seeking to exploit the trust embedded within financial infrastructure, turning legitimate access and transaction processes into mechanisms for moving money.” Its Wealth Management Industry Conditions Analytics 2026 survey of 478 wealth managers found 65 per cent rank cybersecurity as their greatest threat, up from 56 per cent in 2025. “Banks must assume that some defenses will eventually fail and design their operations to prevent a single compromise from becoming a financial catastrophe,” the firm said.

Dan Holmes, VP of product planning and strategy at Feedzai, framed it as a trust test for banks moving into digital assets: “While at the moment they are still two different realms, they are targeted by similar attacks. Finance is built on trust: if traditional banking can’t deliver it when it comes to crypto, it won’t work.”

Who holds the keys

Custody specialists read the same facts as an argument for spreading control. Artem Stopnevich, CEO of The Vault, an EU and Swiss regulated digital asset custodian, said institutions “need direct control over signing systems, access policies and transaction approvals” and that, for custodians, “the challenge is to make sure that compromising one operational system is not enough to move funds.”

Andrew Lazutkin, CTO of self-custody wallet maker Tangem, said the incident shows how custodial models concentrate risk. “With self-custody, users retain direct control of their private keys. When funds are properly secured in an offline wallet, an exchange breach alone does not give attackers access to them,” he said, while conceding that self-custody “does not eliminate risks such as phishing or malware.” Tangem’s own survey of crypto users found 66 per cent consider self-custody important but only 15 per cent use cold wallets.

Paying for it, and keeping customers

Binance says the losses are covered. Varun Datta, founder and CEO of Web3 investor Truth Ventures, said the theft is only half the pressure. After Bybit lost about $1.5 billion in 2025, it processed around $4 billion of withdrawals. “After a major exchange hack, I would watch how much customers withdraw as closely as how much was stolen,” he said. He also warned about what an emergency fund holds: “If an exchange owes customers $1 billion in stablecoins and holds $1 billion in Bitcoin to cover a loss, a 10% Bitcoin fall leaves it $100 million short unless it adds more money.”

Ed Goh, head of trading at liquidity provider B2C2, said volumes and liquidity returned to normal levels once withdrawals resumed. “The question now is whether that recovery holds and trading activity remains stable over the coming weeks,” he said, pointing to perpetual futures open interest relative to rival exchanges as the signal to watch. “For now, Binance Futures remains one of the dominant liquidity pools among centralised exchanges.”

Following the money

About half the haul was frozen, which leaves roughly as much in the attackers’ hands or already moving. Jonathan Benton, founder of crypto asset recovery firm iSanctuary and a former senior UK law enforcement officer, said: “The technology exists to trace stolen funds; however, the challenge is turning that intelligence into rapid, coordinated action before those assets disappear. It needs to be part of the infrastructure.”

B2C2’s head of funding, Mark Jones, described how stolen USDT was taken to lending platform Aave and swapped into ETH, which cannot be frozen at the issuer. “Aave wasn’t hacked. Instead, the exploiter used its normal lending functions,” he said. “That’s why containment has to happen as early as possible, and at the token level, which is far more targeted than the platform level.”

In Westminster, the co-chairs of Parliament’s Crypto and Digital Assets APPG, Lord Vaizey of Didcot and Gurinder Singh Josan CBE MP, called on the UK government to work with international partners “to trace and freeze the remaining funds, disrupt money laundering and identify and sanction those responsible,” and for the National Crime Agency and National Cyber Security Centre to share the lessons with UK businesses. “The immediate priority must be to stop North Korea benefiting from this theft and prevent further attacks.”

The second wave: scams

Security specialists expect criminals to exploit the confusion. NordVPN warned customers on every platform to watch for “an email claiming your funds are at risk, a fake support account offering help or a message urging you to move your cryptocurrency to a ‘safe wallet'”, and to check updates only through the Binance app or a website they already trust. ISACA’s Dimitriadis agreed that high-profile incidents “are often exploited by hackers on other platforms to trick users into taking immediate action that could compromise their crypto assets.”

What comes next

Regulation is likely to follow. In the UK, Capco’s Patel said the hack “puts emphasis on implementation of improved regulations such as the UK’s new Cryptoasset Regime,” while noting that even under the new rules “there is currently a lack of a of FSCS-like measures.”

iSanctuary’s Benton offered the verdict the industry will be judged on: “The future of crypto won’t be decided by how much money enters the market, but by how safe that money is once it’s there.”

title: In Profile: Sid Powell, CEO and Co-Founder at Maple Finance
snippet: Maple Finance chief executive Sid Powell on bringing securitisation onchain, why DeFi is judged by its worst week, and winning over institutional allocators. The post In Profile: Sid Powell, CEO and Co-Founder at Maple Finance appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Sid Powell spent his early career inside the plumbing of traditional credit markets, working on securitisation, corporate finance and credit risk at National Australia Bank before becoming portfolio manager and treasurer at an Australian non-bank lender.

Sid Powell, CEO and co-founder at Maple Finance

In 2019 he co-founded Maple Finance, an onchain asset manager that builds institutional credit infrastructure on public blockchains. The firm says it has originated more than $24 billion in loans and now manages more than $4.6 billion in assets.

In this In Profile, Sid Powell, CEO and co-founder at Maple Finance, discusses bringing securitisation onchain, why DeFi is judged by its worst week, and what it will take for institutional allocators to follow.

Tell us more about your company and its purpose

Maple is an onchain asset manager, meaning we’re a platform that uses blockchain infrastructure to manage both crypto and traditional assets. We build institutional grade credit infrastructure on public blockchains, pairing traditional capital markets fundamentals with the transparency and settlement speed crypto rails make possible. We started in 2019 on the idea that credit markets don’t need to be opaque in order to be safe. Every loan we originate sits on a public transparency page, so lenders can see collateralisation and performance in real time instead of waiting on a quarterly report.

Since 2022 we’ve originated more than $24 billion in loans across multiple market cycles, spanning secured lending and structured credit for institutional borrowers and lenders. More recently, we’ve built products like syrupUSDC and syrupUSDG that bring that same institutional grade yield to a much wider audience, including people on mainstream platforms who never touch decentralised finance (DeFi) directly. The purpose hasn’t changed since day one: make credit markets more transparent and more efficient, without cutting corners on risk.

What are some of your recent achievements you’d like to highlight?

An achievement I’m proudest of this year is launching our own token, syrupUSDG, with Robinhood and Paxos. It went live on Ethereum and on Robinhood Chain at the same time, so retail users had access to institutional-grade onchain yield immediately. It’s our first new syrup product in two years and the clearest signal yet that mainstream fintech is treating onchain infrastructure as credible rather than experimental. To demonstrate the scale, Robinhood alone reported 28.4 million funded customers and $369 billion in platform assets last quarter, and the Global Dollar Network that syrupUSDG plugs into has grown past $3.5 billion in circulation across more than 150 enterprise partners.

We also launched the Kraken Warehouse structure in June, a real, working case study in how DeFi capital gets put to productive economic use. I was particularly proud of this because I came from a securitisation banking background, and one of the original dreams for Maple was to bring securitisation onchain.

And finally, another proud achievement was Fortune naming Maple to its 2026 Crypto Innovators list, which meant a lot for our team.

How did you get into the fintech industry?

After years in traditional finance, I saw first-hand how slow lending can be. At National Australia Bank, I worked across securitisation, corporate finance and credit risk, then as portfolio manager and treasurer at Angle Finance, a non-bank lender funding small and medium businesses across Australia.

Both roles put me inside the plumbing of credit markets: structuring deals, managing risk, and watching how long it takes to verify collateral or settle a facility when everything runs through intermediaries and manual processes. I was looking for the next technology shift in finance and as I started learning more about blockchain and smart contracts, I could see that this would be a major platform shift which would enable new winners to emerge. This presented an exciting opportunity to try and build one of those winners. So co-founding Maple was a chance to build the credit market I wished I’d had on the other side of those deals: transparent, faster to settle, and just as disciplined about risk.

What’s the best thing about working in the fintech industry?

The best thing about working in fintech is watching formerly slow processes happen in real time. In traditional credit, verifying collateral, confirming a loan is performing, and settling a transaction can each take days. But on blockchain, that same information is visible instantly to anyone who wants to check it. That shift, from “trust me” to see-for-yourself, is what got me excited about this space, and it’s still what excites me most about it now. The other part is the pace of convergence. A few years ago, a bank or a brokerage building on public blockchain rails was a novelty. Now it’s a live product decision inside firms managing large volumes of real customer money. Being close to that shift, and building some of the infrastructure it runs on, is a front-row seat into the future of finance.

What frustrates you most about the fintech industry?

The industry still gets judged by its worst week. April was a rough month for DeFi broadly, with security incidents at other protocols driving real losses, and it coloured how a lot of people talked about the whole space for weeks afterwards. That’s a fair thing for outsiders to be cautious about. What’s frustrating is when caution turns into “this is all the same thing,” when in reality risk management, transparency and underwriting standards vary enormously from one platform to the next. We built our business on being the more conservative, mature and transparent option, and it’s frustrating when that distinction gets flattened in the coverage.

How have your previous roles influenced your career?

My background shaped how I operate now and I owe a lot to the mentors I had during my time in banking. Securitisation at NAB taught me a lot of fundamentals about structuring deals, analysing cash flows and downside protection. It’s fundamentally about breaking assets into cash flows and understanding exactly what’s backing a set of obligations, which isn’t far from how we think about structuring loans and collateral at Maple; it’s just moved onchain. Credit risk work forces a certain discipline, ensuring you don’t get comfortable with an exposure just because it hasn’t gone wrong yet. That instinct shaped how conservative we’ve tried to be about risk management and transparency at Maple.

My work in treasury and portfolio management, including managing funding, liquidity and a live book of loans to small businesses, is the piece that translates most directly to running Maple day to day. We balance growth against risk, and never assume a portfolio performing today will keep performing without active management. I don’t think I’d run this business the same way without having sat on both sides of that table first.

What’s the best mistake you’ve ever made?

The most useful mistake we’ve made was mistaking optionality for progress. Early on, we tried to advance too many initiatives at once. It felt ambitious, but it diluted focus and slowed execution. The lesson was that conviction only matters if it is concentrated. Since then, we’ve run Maple around fewer, higher-conviction priorities, with clear ownership and a much higher bar for taking on anything new. We don’t spend much time regretting mistakes. We extract the lesson, change the system, and move on.

What has the future got in store for your company?

At Maple, we’re excited about what’s ahead. Expect to see more of the fintech distribution model we proved out with Robinhood, and more institutions bringing real credit structures onchain the way we’re doing with our current facilities. I already said publicly that “every fintech will offer yield on stablecoin balances within the next two years.” Maple will become the credit manager behind most of that yield. On the institutional side, we expect to keep seeing traditional finance players move real credit structures onchain. That powerful shift towards onchain credit will soon simply be how a deal gets done. Maple is pioneering the future of onchain asset management, one deal at a time.

What are the next key talking points or challenges for your industry as a whole?

Regulatory clarity is the big challenge for DeFi. Guidance on how stablecoins get classified has become very real this year, and you can see the effect directly, with firms like Robinhood and Tempo shipping products that would have been hard to justify building eighteen months ago. The next challenge is proving that clarity was worth waiting for.

The next big bridge for the industry to cross is how we get institutional allocators to start deploying onchain. This is what will drive the next order of magnitude of growth. In a lot of ways, the blockchain space is still reliant on early adopters among retail and high net worth. Bitcoin ETFs, vaults and tokenised stocks are helping to familiarise institutional investors but as of yet, examples of them allocating onchain are isolated and rare.

The other conversation the industry needs to keep having, honestly, is about risk management standards. This year’s DeFi hacks showed that not every protocol manages collateral and underwriting in the same way, and the ones that do it well need to be louder about how, not just that they didn’t get hit. Transparency has to be a selling point the industry competes on, to help it build the trust it deserves.

title: Y3S Embeds Curvestone AI Into CRM for Mortgage Compliance Oversight
snippet: Specialist Mortgage Group has deployed Curvestone's AI platform across its advice and quality-control process to meet growing FCA suitability demands. The post Y3S Embeds Curvestone AI Into CRM for Mortgage Compliance Oversight appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Specialist Mortgage Group, the Cardiff-based group behind Y3S Loans, Y3S Bridging and Commercial, and Chase Blue Loans, has deployed the Curvestone AI compliance platform across its advice and quality-control workflow. The integration, which runs via API into the group’s existing CRM, is live across four discrete checks and applies to every case the group processes.

Curvestone ingests call transcripts, emails, WhatsApp and text messages, credit files and applicant data, then scores each file against the group’s internal policies as a case progresses. The four checks now live cover document completeness (what the platform calls shopping list validation), vulnerability assessment, Land Registry report review, and an advice suitability assessment that runs each case against more than 100 validation points. Each report is generated in approximately five minutes and cites the underlying evidence for every finding.

Consumer Duty in practice

The deployment carries direct regulatory weight. The FCA‘s Consumer Duty, which came into full force in July 2023 and extended to closed products in July 2024, places explicit obligations on firms to identify and support vulnerable customers. The regulator has also recently completed a distribution review of the second charge mortgage market, with suitability rather than eligibility at the centre of its scrutiny. For a firm operating across 40 to 50 advisers, consistent vulnerability identification at the case level is no longer a best-practice aspiration; it is a compliance requirement with audit trail expectations attached.

Barney Drake, chief executive of Specialist Mortgage Group, said the previous approach to vulnerability assessment was handled at adviser level and maintaining consistency across the team was considerably harder. “Now it’s driven by our policy, and takes minutes to present all evidence to the advisor, who then makes the final call,” he said. Drake added that the cost of the platform is comparable to employing a person to carry out the same work, but that the output is consistent across every case.

Dawid Kotur, founder and chief executive of Curvestone AI, said the group’s existing commitment to checking 100 per cent of cases placed it ahead of much of the market, and that the platform’s role was to make that oversight consistent, evidenced and fast.

Scale without headcount

The operational logic of the deployment is as much a capacity argument as a compliance one. Specialist Mortgage Group has run quality-control checks on every case for close to a decade. As the group grows, maintaining that coverage without proportional headcount growth requires either process change or tooling. Curvestone’s pitch is that by running inside the existing CRM rather than requiring a parallel system, the platform avoids the workflow disruption that typically slows adoption of compliance tooling.

That framing places Curvestone in a market that has seen growing investment in AI-powered regtech, particularly in tools designed to make Consumer Duty documentation auditable at scale. Larger mortgage networks and lenders have been investing in similar capabilities, and the FCA’s continued focus on the advice and distribution chain in second charge lending means the pressure on smaller, specialist brokers to demonstrate the same rigour is increasing.

Curvestone completed a £3 million seed round in December 2025. It did not disclose a valuation. The company is headquartered in Holborn, London, and describes its focus as AI workflow tooling for complex, high-stakes processes in regulated industries.

title: BNPL bolsters holiday budgets: survey
snippet: Younger shoppers favor buy now, pay later loans more than their older counterparts, but BNPL companies draw consumers across income brackets, a survey finds.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

Younger shoppers favor buy now, pay later loans more than their older counterparts, but BNPL companies draw consumers across income brackets, a survey finds.

        

            

        Published Nov. 2, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                Shoppers wait to enter a store at the Woodbury Commons premium outlets mall on Nov. 25, 2022 in Woodbury, New York.
            
        
            Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

During the 2026 holiday season, a fifth of consumers said they’ll use buy now, pay later providers more than they did last year, according to a survey by the Electronic Transactions Association and TSG, The Strawhecker Group, a payments consulting firm. While a quarter said their BNPL usage will remain the same, nearly half (47%) said they don’t anticipate using BNPL payments at all.

Among people who like using BNPL services, 52% said the payment method allows them to manage large expenses, while 45% use it for unexpected purchases, the survey of 1,099 consumers found.

As for consumers who eschew BNPL options, 73% said they don’t like accruing debt, and 55% don’t want to risk paying high fees or interest payments, per the annual survey, which was released Wednesday.

Dive Insight:

The survey by the ETA and TSG — which gathered responses from U.S. consumers across genders, income levels, generations and geographic areas — suggests that consumers’ perceptions of BNPL payments vary by generation and income level. 

When asked how they felt about their BNPL purchases over the past few months, about four in ten (37%) of consumers across income levels and generations viewed BNPL services favorably, compared to 36% with an unfavorable view. 

While 47% of millennials viewed BNPL payments favorably, 39% of Gen Zers, 38% of Gen Xers and 24% of Baby Boomers said the same. Meanwhile, about a third (35%) of low-income and high-income consumers like BNPL payments, compared to 40% of middle-income consumers who prefer the payment method, the survey found. 

The survey also shed light on which new payment methods consumers have tried over the 12 months. 

At the top of the list was tap-to-pay at 53%, followed by digital wallets (31%) and peer-to-peer apps (28%). By contrast, only 9% said they had tried BNPL in the past year, and cryptocurrencies were lowest at 3% during that same period, the survey found.

The survey tracked a similar pattern from prior years for the payment methods consumers use regularly. 

Among the payment methods consumers said they used regularly, tap-to-pay ranked first at 81%, followed by digital wallets (61%) and peer-to-peer apps (60%). About a fifth (21%) of survey respondents said they used BNPL services regularly; cryptocurrency payments came in last again at only 8%, per the survey results. 

“Convenience and familiarity are converting trial into repeat behavior more effectively than novelty alone,” the report said. “Once consumers try tap-to-pay, digital wallets, and P2P apps, a large share continue using them; driving the first successful transaction remains an important adoption lever.”

Along with TSG’s and the Electronic Transactions Association’s findings, other surveys suggest that consumers perceive BNPL services as a tool for spreading out their payments. In a recent PayPal Holdings survey of 2,005 adults, about six in ten consumers reported leaning toward BNPL payments to extend their holiday budgets and control their spending.

Consumers turned to BNPL payments last year to divvy up their purchases, Block subsidiary Afterpay said earlier this year. During the 2025 holiday season, the company noted that most (96%) of its customers who used its installment payment services for Black Friday and Cyber Monday shopping had repaid their debts early or on time.

title: FIS, Toast CFOs exit
snippet: The chief financial officers are leaving the payments players as the companies grapple with separate challenges.
fullText:
Fidelity National Information Services and Toast separately disclosed that their chief financial officers are exiting, as they also announced third-quarter earnings results. 

At FIS, which provides payments services to banking and capital markets clients, the company announced the departure of James Kehoe, with no further explanation. Alexandra “Alex” Brooks will step into the CFO post on an interim basis starting Thursday as the company begins a search for a permanent replacement, according to a Wednesday press release.

The CFO change at Jacksonville, Florida-based FIS landed as the company adjusted its financial forecasts due to unexpected changes in the outlook for recurring revenue, citing new factors that are dragging on that income.

The shifts were mainly related to changed expectations at some of its banking clients as those customers encounter implementation delays and, in some cases, work through acquisition activity, CEO Stephanie Ferris explained on a webcast with analysts Wednesday. The change is happening as some customers move from services with more traditional licenses to the company’s more updated subscription software services, she said.

“Over the course of the third quarter, we started to see some client-directed conversion delays, primarily in our larger client base, and some impacts from the timing around large bank consolidation,” Ferris said on the webcast.

FIS divests prepaid business

She also noted that the company would invest in technology and security to assist clients with implementations and to prioritize cyber work.

“These factors will weigh on our results in the fourth quarter in 2027, and we expect them to largely fade in 2028,” Ferris said. 

FIS also disclosed during the third-quarter report that it had sold what it referred to as a “non-core, prepaid asset” for $100 million. A spokesperson for the company didn’t immediately respond to requests for more information about the unit or the buyer.

Kehoe has been with FIS since August 2023, joining shortly after Ferris became CEO in January of that year. Together, they took the company through a $24.25 billion sale last year of its merchants services business Worldpay to Global Payments, and the $13.5 billion acquisition of a card issuer business from Global Payments.

FIS reported third-quarter adjusted net earnings rose 5.3% to $831 million as operating revenue climbed 29%, on an adjusted basis, to $3.37 billion, according to the company’s earnings press release.

At Toast, the digital payments processor said that its president and chief financial officer, Elena Gomez, will leave her posts at the end of the year. Michael Senno, who has served as Toast’s senior vice president of finance, will become CFO at that time, the company said.

Gomez, who has been at Toast since May 2021 and guided the company through its initial public offering that year, said in the company’s earnings press release that it’s time “to take a break before my next chapter.”

Toast CEO criticizes lawsuit

Meanwhile, during a webcast with analysts on Tuesday, Toast’s CEO, Aman Narang, continued to make a case for fighting a lawsuit brought by the Federal Trade Commission and states last week. The federal and state regulators alleged in their lawsuit that the company exacted “hidden fees” and “unauthorized charges” from both merchants and consumers. 

Narang defended the contracts Toast negotiates with every restaurant, and other merchants, to provide services in the business-to-business industry. 

The lawsuit turns on the Federal Trade Commission Act and the Restore Online Shoppers’ Confidence Act, barring companies from misleading customers. The regulators said Toast made “false or misleading claims” regarding its subscription and financing services; failed to make required disclosures; didn’t provide simple ways for customers to cancel their subscription; and charged customers without their consent. 

“We are incredibly disappointed with the FTC's decision to file the suit,” Narang told analysts on the earnings webcast. “We've been engaged with them and cooperating with them really over the past year, and fundamentally believe their application of ROSCA is unprecedented for custom contracts in B2B.”

Narang posited that the enforcement action on that basis could impact the entire industry. “If ROSCA were to apply to B2B custom negotiated contracts in a B2B context, it would have huge implications for, really, the whole industry and business contracts in general,” Narang contended. “We have a lot of confidence in our business practices and are ready to defend ourselves.” 

Toast reported third-quarter net income rose 60% to $169 million as revenue increased 21% to $1.98 billion, according to the earnings press release.

The CFOs at both FIS and Toast said they’ll continue to work with the companies to transfer their duties to their successors.

title: Who is Accountable When an AI Agent Makes a Payment?
snippet: As AI agents start making payments, xpate's Sofia Khatsernova says providers must set limits, trace autonomous decisions and settle liability in advance. The post Who is Accountable When an AI Agent Makes a Payment? appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
As AI agents begin to make payments on people’s behalf, payment providers face a question that cyber security alone cannot answer: what stops an agent from making a transaction its user never agreed to, and who carries the liability if it does?

Sofia Khatsernova, legal function owner at xpate

The concern is widely shared. Some 78 per cent of financial institutions expect fraud to increase significantly as agentic commerce grows, while 85 per cent say their current systems and scaling plans are not prepared for it, figures shared by xpate, the global payments and banking platform, during Cybersecurity Awareness Month.

Sofia Khatsernova, legal function owner at xpate, argues that autonomy for AI in finance has to come with limits written in from the start.

“You can’t give AI autonomy in finance without building in constraints. Legal and compliance teams will need to define clear boundaries around what these systems can do, how decisions are documented, and where liability sits,” she said.

Consent that keeps pace

For Khatsernova, the bigger shift is in how consent works. A single agreement at sign-up is not enough when software is acting on a customer’s behalf over time.

“Consent also needs to evolve, not as a one-time agreement, but as something more dynamic and granular, with built-in safeguards that prevent autonomous systems from acting beyond the authority users have granted them,” she said.

That points to three practical tasks for payment providers: setting clear limits on what an AI agent may initiate, being able to trace and document the decisions an autonomous system makes, and settling in advance where liability falls when an agent executes a payment without proper authorisation.

As agent-initiated payments move from pilots towards everyday use, the providers that answer those questions early are likely to find it easier to win the trust of both regulators and customers.

Riverside Payments and its affiliates agreed to pay $600,000 to resolve allegations they misled small businesses about processing costs.

        

            

        Published Nov. 4, 2026
